prize_parts.citation: for foundational contributions to the theory of nominal rigidities and policy rules that underpin the modern analysis of monetary policy

statement.case_for: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework are the working core of how monetary policy is modelled, taught and conducted. Calvo's time-dependent pricing is the building block of the New Keynesian Phillips curve. Taylor's staggered contracts and policy rule changed how rule-based policy is discussed and evaluated. Woodford turned these pieces into a microfounded framework for normative analysis of policy. The work is 25 to 45 years old, has been tested in the post-2008 and post-2021 episodes, and is still the reference framework even where it is being extended with heterogeneity and financial frictions. These three names are the most separable originators of distinct core elements: pricing, contracts and rules, and the synthesis. That separability matters more to me than how many colleagues rank the field first.
statement.case_against: Credit in this field is diffuse. Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gertler and Smets made major theoretical and empirical contributions, so any three-person cut leaves out serious contributors. The Taylor rule is closer to a robust empirical regularity than to a deep theorem. The framework's performance after 2008 and in the 2021-23 inflation is contested. The strongest alternatives, B007 and B026, have cleaner attribution to two names each, and that is a real argument against my first choice.

responses.point: Andersson proposes Taylor, Woodford and Gali for B012. He sees Gali's canonical New Keynesian model and its empirical evaluation as part of a defensible core, and he flags that any three-person cut is contestable.
responses.response: I take the Gali case seriously. His work on the New Keynesian Phillips curve and on empirical evaluation of the model is substantial and arguably the best bridge between theory and data in this field. I still prefer Calvo to Gali because Calvo's 1983 pricing model is the originating element that the New Keynesian Phillips curve builds on, and Woodford's synthesis and Gali's work both rest on it. I would prefer a prize that credits the origin to one that credits only later syntheses. I agree with Andersson that the choice is a judgement call, and I would not oppose a Woodford-Gali-Taylor configuration if the Committee judges Gali's integrated contribution to outweigh the priority of the pricing model.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B007 first and adds Gertler to Kiyotaki and Moore, arguing that the financial-accelerator and intermediary-friction work extended the mechanism into a large quantitative literature.
responses.response: I agree that the quantitative macro-finance literature is a main reason B007 matters. I still think the cleaner attribution is to Kiyotaki and Moore, because the collateral-constraint amplification mechanism is a well-defined two-author discovery. Gertler's strongest contributions run through the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator, which partly overlaps with Bernanke's 2022 prize, and through the monetary-policy work credited under B012. Adding him would blur the discovery and place his credit in two ballots. That is why I keep B007 as an alternative and not as part of my preferred configuration, and why I do not add Gertler to B012. Krusell is my frequent co-author, so I flag this as a disclosed relationship, not as an argument.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B026 first. She argues that firm heterogeneity and selection changed how gains from trade, reallocation and productivity are understood, that it is a distinct advance after Krugman's 2008 prize, and that Melitz and Helpman are the right pair.
responses.response: I accept the distinctness argument. Melitz (2003) and Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple introduced selection and the extensive margin, which Krugman's earlier prize did not cover. I also agree that Redding's role is mostly extension. My remaining reservation is attribution. Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum made parallel empirical and quantitative contributions that are not credited on this ballot, and Helpman also appears under the trade-politics entry. B026 is therefore not as clean as the two-name proposal suggests. Still, on scientific grounds it is a stronger alternative than I weighted it at opening, and I list it as one of my two alternatives.

responses.point: Dreber-Almenberg ranks B001 first for its durable influence on finance, law and development. She states that the legal-origins results face robustness, measurement and causal-interpretation concerns.
responses.response: I share both halves of her assessment. The law-and-finance programme opened a large empirical field with very wide reach. Her own caution about replicability and revised measures, such as the anti-director index, is the main reason I keep it fifth. A prize rewards a result that has held up under scrutiny. The legal-origins thesis has been heavily qualified, and four co-authors compete for three places, so I would want the Committee to resolve the Vishny question and the robustness evidence before it moves higher.

uncertainties: Whether Gali or Christiano and Eichenbaum, rather than Calvo or Taylor, should be among the three named laureates for B012.
How much weight the Committee should give the framework's mixed performance in the post-2008 and 2021-23 episodes compared with its lasting influence on policy practice.
Whether the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises makes B007 look too close to recognised ground, and whether Gertler belongs in a macro-finance award.
Whether Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum should be considered alongside Melitz and Helpman for B026.
Whether the Committee prefers a clean two-name attribution (B007, B026) to a more influential but diffusely credited field (B012).
statement.conflict_note: The supplied profile shows no collaboration or institutional tie to Calvo, Taylor or Woodford, nor to Kiyotaki, Moore, Melitz or Helpman. I disclose that I co-authored with committee members Krusell, Boppart and Friberg, and that I am an IIES colleague of Krusell and Boppart. These ties could matter when I weigh their views, but none of the proposed laureates is a co-author. My research field is macroeconomics, which is close to B012 and B007. For B009 I note only possible proximity to the Stockholm economics community, which the profile does not document. These connections are disclosed, not adjudicated.
